# Results — Study 951 (The Crossover Rung) on the real daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The question: is the **BBB/BB
boundary** the best-paid rung of the US corporate credit ladder? Every rung's daily
total-return series is turned **excess-of-cash** (minus BIL's total return) and then
regressed on two excess factors — **IEF** for duration and **SPY** for equity beta — so the
race is not simply won by whoever carries the most risk. The headline statistic is the
two-factor alpha on the **return difference** between two rungs, with a Newey-West HAC *t*.
Daily total-return closes (`yfinance`, `auto_adjust=True`). As-of **2026-06-30** (the
partial current month is dropped).*

**Proxies and assumptions** (none of these are tape): the crossover rung is proxied by the
**fallen-angel** ETFs **ANGL** and **FALN** — there is no free daily total-return tape of a
literal BBB−/BB+ index, and a fallen-angel fund is event-tilted and longer-duration than the
crossover universe as a whole; **IEF/SPY** are a two-factor risk adjustment, not a full
credit-factor model; **BIL** is the cash leg; the short-leg **borrow rate** in the long/short
expression is an assumption and is swept 0 → 100 bps. ETF total-return closes are already net
of the fund expense ratio, so no fee is charged twice. **The IEF/SPY betas are fitted in
sample** — full-window OLS, and the alpha is the in-sample intercept. That is the standard
attribution form, and the fitted hedge is never traded (both tradable expressions below hold
raw funds), but it means the alpha describes the sample rather than a return anyone banked
out of sample. All three head-to-head pairs are run on the **same ANGL-gated window** so the
rows are comparable; where a longer window exists it is reported separately and labelled.

## Data stamp

| Legs | Window | n days | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| AGG, LQD, ANGL, HYG + IEF, SPY, BIL | 2012-04-11 → 2026-06-30 | 3,575 | Fingerprint `b2e46afc7601` |

ANGL's 2012 inception gates the headline window. Cross-check tapes: **FALN** (2016-06→, a
second fallen-angel fund) and **USHY** (2017-10→, a second broad high-yield fund).

## The ladder — excess-of-cash, then duration- and equity-adjusted

| Rung | Excess Sharpe | Excess return | Vol | Max DD (abs) | Alpha vs IEF+SPY | HAC *t* | β IEF | β SPY | R² |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **AGG** (aggregate) | +0.113 | +0.55%/yr | 4.86% | −18.4% | −0.48%/yr | −0.94 | 0.71 | 0.07 | 0.84 |
| **LQD** (investment grade) | +0.241 | +1.89%/yr | 7.82% | −25.0% | −0.67%/yr | −0.49 | 0.97 | 0.18 | 0.67 |
| **ANGL** (crossover) | **+0.602** | +5.57%/yr | 9.25% | **−29.3%** | +0.84%/yr | +0.42 | 0.34 | 0.35 | 0.39 |
| **HYG** (broad high yield) | +0.437 | +3.42%/yr | 7.82% | −22.0% | −1.67%/yr | −1.23 | 0.27 | 0.37 | 0.62 |

The **raw** shape is exactly the folklore's: reward-per-unit-risk rises up the ladder, peaks
at the crossover rung (excess Sharpe **+0.602**) and then *falls* into broad high yield
(+0.437). The ladder has a hump, and the hump sits on the boundary. But **no single rung's
alpha clears |*t*| = 2** on its own — the factor adjustment eats the levels, and what is
left is a comparison between rungs, not an absolute premium.

## The head-to-head — two-factor alpha on the return difference

All three pairs on the **same** ANGL-gated window (2012-04-12 → 2026-06-30, n = 3,574), so
the rows can be read against each other.

| Pair | Alpha (adjusted) | HAC *t* | Raw excess difference | HAC *t* (raw) | n |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **ANGL − HYG** (boundary vs deep HY) | **+2.51%/yr** | **+2.01** | +2.15%/yr | +1.96 | 3,574 |
| **ANGL − LQD** (boundary vs IG) | +1.51%/yr | +1.15 | +3.68%/yr | +2.09 | 3,574 |
| HYG − LQD (deep HY vs IG) | −1.00%/yr | −0.83 | +1.53%/yr | +0.92 | 3,574 |

*Aside, labelled:* HYG − LQD is the one pair that does not need ANGL, so it can also be run
on its own longest (BIL-gated) window, 2007-05-31 → 2026-06-30, n = 4,801 — there it reads
**+0.05%/yr, *t* = +0.03**. Both readings say the same thing (the IG→HY step pays nothing
risk-adjusted); the 19-year number is *not* mixed into the table above, because a row
measured on a different sample is not a comparison.

So the ladder claim splits in two, and only half of it half-survives:

- Against **broad high yield** the crossover rung earns **+2.51%/yr** of duration- and
  equity-adjusted alpha at *t* = **+2.01** — sitting *exactly* on the desk's bar, not above it.
- Against **investment grade** the same rung earns **+1.51%/yr** at *t* = **+1.15**. The IG
  side of the boundary — the half of the claim that would make it a *rung*, not just a
  better high-yield fund — is not there. Its raw difference (+3.68%/yr, *t* = +2.09) is pure
  risk compensation: the adjustment removes 59% of it.
- The **HYG − LQD** step is a dead loss (−1.00%/yr, *t* = −0.83 on the common window;
  +0.05%/yr, *t* = +0.03 on the 19-year one): once you adjust for duration and equity beta,
  moving from investment grade to broad high yield paid nothing at all, on either sample.

## Bootstrap CI on the head-to-head alpha (2,000 draws, 21-day blocks)

Blocks are resampled *jointly* across the difference series and the factor tape, so the
interval reflects estimation error in the betas as well as the intercept.

| Pair | Alpha | 95% CI | share < 0 |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| ANGL − HYG | +2.51%/yr | [+0.38%, +4.74%] | 1.3% |
| ANGL − LQD | +1.51%/yr | [−0.61%, +3.90%] | 8.0% |

The high-yield leg's interval clears zero — barely, with the lower bound at +0.38%/yr. The
investment-grade leg's does not.

## Robustness 1 — the era cut (split 2019-01-01)

| Pair | Era | n | Alpha | HAC *t* | Raw difference |
|---|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| ANGL − HYG | 2012–2018 | 1,691 | **+4.47%/yr** | **+2.63** | +2.82%/yr |
| ANGL − HYG | 2019–2026 | 1,882 | +1.50%/yr | +0.92 | +1.51%/yr |
| ANGL − LQD | 2012–2018 | 1,691 | +3.94%/yr | +2.02 | +3.88%/yr |
| ANGL − LQD | 2019–2026 | 1,882 | −0.05%/yr | −0.03 | +3.51%/yr |

The premium is a **first-era phenomenon**, and by a factor of three. This is the single most
damaging cut, because the late era is *not* a quiet one for the mechanism: it contains the
March-2020 fallen-angel wave (Ford, Occidental, Kraft Heinz — the largest downgrade cohort in
history). The mechanism fired hard and the adjusted premium still only reached *t* = +0.92.

## Robustness 2 — the calendar year and the one-year-out jackknife

Per-year compounded excess-return difference, ANGL − HYG (unadjusted, the lived experience):

| 2012 | 2013 | 2014 | 2015 | **2016** | 2017 | 2018 | 2019 | **2020** | 2021 | 2022 | 2023 | 2024 | 2025 | 2026 H1 |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| +2.12 | +1.15 | +0.63 | +3.60 | **+10.65** | +3.41 | −3.92 | +3.48 | **+8.48** | +2.98 | −3.74 | +0.82 | −1.77 | +0.47 | +0.58 |

Two years carry it: **2016** (the energy-and-mining downgrade wave recovering off the
February lows) and **2020** (the COVID fallen-angel wave). Delete calendar years one at a
time and re-estimate:

- **|*t*| ≥ 2 survives only 5 of 15 single-year deletions.** Dropping 2016 alone takes the
  alpha to **+1.84%/yr at *t* = +1.43**; dropping 2015 gives *t* = +1.79; dropping 2012,
  2013, 2017, 2019, 2021, 2023 or 2026 all land between *t* = +1.79 and +1.94.
- Dropping **both** crisis-recovery years (2016 and 2020) leaves **+1.55%/yr at *t* = +1.61**
  over the remaining 3,069 days — the same sign, 38% smaller, and not significant.

A premium that only clears the bar when both of its two best years are in the sample is a
premium that has not cleared the bar.

## Robustness 3 — HAC bandwidth and independent tapes

The bandwidth sweep is honest in the *unhelpful* direction: the *t* is at its lowest at the
short bandwidths and rises with the kernel, so the headline (default rule-of-thumb, 8 lags)
is not a cherry-picked wide window.

| HAC lags | 5 | 8 (default) | 10 | 21 | 42 |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| *t* on ANGL − HYG | +1.95 | **+2.01** | +2.01 | +2.25 | +2.54 |

Swap either leg for its sibling fund and the premium all but vanishes — but read the *window*
column before drawing a conclusion from it:

| Pair | Window | n | Alpha | HAC *t* |
|---|---|--:|--:|--:|
| ANGL − HYG (headline) | 2012-04 → 2026-06 | 3,574 | +2.51%/yr | +2.01 |
| **FALN − USHY** (both legs swapped) | 2017-10 → 2026-06 | 2,178 | **+0.63%/yr** | **+0.48** |
| FALN − HYG (crossover leg swapped) | 2016-06 → 2026-06 | 2,519 | +1.78%/yr | +1.34 |
| ANGL − USHY (HY leg swapped) | 2017-10 → 2026-06 | 2,178 | +0.18%/yr | +0.14 |

**How much of that is the funds, and how much is the window?** Almost all of it is the
window. Run *all four* pairs on the one window the four funds share (2017-10 → 2026-06,
n = 2,178) and the **headline pair itself** collapses:

| Same window, four pairs | ANGL − HYG (headline) | FALN − HYG | FALN − USHY | ANGL − USHY |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Alpha | **+0.96%/yr** | +1.42%/yr | +0.63%/yr | +0.18%/yr |
| HAC *t* | **+0.67** | +0.97 | +0.48 | +0.14 |

So the sibling-fund test is **not a third, independent failure** — it is mostly the era cut
restated. Changing funds moves the alpha by about 1.2 pp; changing the window moves the
headline pair from +2.51%/yr to +0.96%/yr on its own. The honest reading is that this study
has **two** distinct pieces of adverse evidence, not three: the premium is carried by a
handful of early downgrade-wave years (jackknife + era cut), and the fund-identity noise on
top of that is roughly as large as what is left. On the
FALN/USHY-gated 2017-10 → 2026-06 window (n = 2,179) the five-fund ladder is *entirely*
negative-alpha and the ordering survives only faintly:

| Rung | LQD | **FALN** | ANGL | USHY | HYG |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Excess Sharpe | +0.041 | **+0.364** | +0.312 | +0.311 | +0.244 |
| Alpha (HAC *t*) | −1.12% (−0.56) | −1.01% (−0.38) | −1.46% (−0.55) | −1.64% (−0.87) | −2.42% (−1.33) |

The hump shape is still visible — both crossover funds sit above both broad-HY funds by
excess Sharpe — but every alpha is negative and every |*t*| < 1.4. The *premium* is not
measurable on this window.

## The two tradable expressions

**Expression A — own the crossover fund instead of the broad high-yield fund.** No shorting,
no borrow, no timing: a single fund swap inside a high-yield sleeve you already hold. The
switch is charged on **both** sides — sell HYG *and* buy ANGL, 2 × 5 bps one-way — amortised
over 14 years, which is ~0.007%/yr of drag.

| | Excess Sharpe | Excess return | Vol | Max DD (abs) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| HYG | +0.437 | +3.42%/yr | 7.82% | −22.0% |
| **ANGL** (net of the switch) | **+0.602** | +5.56%/yr | 9.25% | **−29.3%** |

The reward-per-risk gain (+0.165) is real and essentially free of friction. The **admission
price is drawdown**: the crossover fund fell 7.3 pp further in March 2020 and carries 18%
more volatility. This is a risk-composition change, not a free lunch.

**Expression B — the pure spread (long ANGL, short HYG), dollar-neutral, reset monthly.**
Weights implied by the closes through the last trading day of month *t* are acted on at
*t*+1 (the study's single execution lag), where a 5 bps one-way cost × NAV is charged on the
drift turnover (0.38× per year). The short leg pays borrow, which is an assumption; it also
pays HYG's distributions across to the lender, which is *not* an assumption — both legs are
total-return series, so that cost is charged by the tape itself:

| Borrow (assumed) | Alpha | HAC *t* | Mean | Sharpe |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 bps | +2.53%/yr | +2.11 | +2.14%/yr | +0.342 |
| 25 bps | +2.28%/yr | +1.90 | +1.89%/yr | +0.302 |
| **50 bps** | **+2.03%/yr** | **+1.69** | +1.64%/yr | +0.262 |
| 100 bps | +1.53%/yr | +1.28 | +1.14%/yr | +0.182 |

At a realistic ETF borrow of ~50 bps the pure spread's *t* is **+1.69** and its standalone
Sharpe is +0.26. Shorting the ladder rung below you is not how this is collected.

## Synthetic control (machinery proof only — never supports the stamp)

A three-rung ladder built from a duration factor and an equity factor, with a **planted
+3.00%/yr** premium on the crossover rung: the estimator recovers **+3.58%/yr at *t* = +4.64**
with the right factor loadings. On the zero-alpha null across 8 seeds the recovered alpha
averages **+0.10%/yr** (sd 0.60%) and |*t*| ≥ 2 fires **0/8**. The estimator finds a real
premium when one is there and stays quiet when it is not — so the real-tape borderline
reading is a property of the credit tape, not of the harness.

## Verdict

- **Signal — Weak.** The *shape* of the claim is right: the excess-Sharpe ladder does hump at
  the crossover rung (+0.602 vs +0.437 for broad high yield and +0.241 for investment grade),
  and the sign of the crossover premium is positive in every cut, every era and all four
  fund-pair combinations. What fails is the **robustness bar**. (i) The headline alpha vs
  broad high yield is *t* = **+2.01** — on the line, not past it — and it survives only **5 of
  15** single-year deletions; dropping 2016 alone drops it to *t* = +1.43, and dropping both
  crisis-recovery years to *t* = +1.61. (ii) The whole premium is first-era: **+4.47%/yr
  (*t* = +2.63)** before 2019 against **+1.50%/yr (*t* = +0.92)** after, despite the late era
  containing the largest fallen-angel wave on record. (iii) Swapping both legs for their
  sibling funds (FALN − USHY) gives **+0.63%/yr at *t* = +0.48** — but that is *not* a third
  independent failure: on the same 2017-2026 window the headline pair itself reads only
  +0.96%/yr (*t* = +0.67), so the sibling test is mostly (ii) restated, with about 1.2 pp of
  genuine fund-identity noise on top. Counted honestly this study has **two** pieces of
  adverse evidence, not three — and two is enough. (iv) The other half of the
  ladder claim — that the boundary also out-earns *investment grade* on a risk-adjusted
  basis — is simply absent: **+1.51%/yr at *t* = +1.15**, bootstrap CI [−0.61%, +3.90%], and
  **−0.05%/yr** in the recent era. So: the boundary is the best-paid rung *by raw
  reward-per-risk*, but only against the rung below it, only in the first half of the
  sample, and only at the significance bar rather than beyond it. Sign right, robustness
  short — Weak. *Survivorship: all six funds are living, asset-gathering ETFs; the
  crossover funds that failed to launch or were closed are not on this tape, and the
  index-reconstitution history inside each fund is not observable here. One US credit
  history, 14 years, two downgrade waves.*
- **Tradability — Fragile.** Not a cost Mirage: Expression A is a one-off fund swap with a
  ~0.7 bp/yr amortised drag charged on *both* legs of the switch, fees already inside the
  tape, no borrow and no timing, and it
  did deliver +0.165 of excess Sharpe over the full window. Fragile because what you buy is
  a **risk-composition change wearing a premium's clothes** — a 7.3 pp deeper worst
  drawdown (−29.3% vs −22.0%) and 18% more volatility for a premium that is
  regime-contingent (three times smaller after 2018), event-driven (two years carry the
  whole thing) and not reproducible on the sibling-fund pair. The pure long/short
  expression is worse: at a realistic 50 bps borrow its *t* falls to +1.69 and its Sharpe to
  +0.26. Hold it as a *tilt* inside a high-yield sleeve if you want the downgrade-wave
  exposure; do not size it as a harvested premium.
